content: 1. To verify the achievement of hepatitis B control targets, countries must demonstrate at least five years of sustained high coverage of the HepB3 vaccine at both national and subnational levels, meeting the Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS) targets. Additional data may be required to assess coverage before and after impact assessment surveys. 2. Supplementary information may be necessary, as multiple lines of evidence will be evaluated to confirm that the target has been achieved. These lines of evidence must be consistent in supporting the conclusion. 3. Other sources of information should be provided if available, particularly if measures such as antenatal testing for hepatitis B virus (HBV) and prophylaxis for infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers have been implemented. This is especially relevant for countries that have not introduced a universal birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine. 4. Relevant information may include national policies and guidelines on antenatal HBV testing, coverage of antenatal testing, prevalence of HBsAg among pregnant women, coverage of timely birth dose (TBD) vaccination among infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers, availability and coverage of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) for these infants, and data from post-vaccination serological testing (PVST). 5. Surveillance for acute hepatitis, particularly among children, provides critical information on the incidence and trends of acute infections and associated risk factors. However, most new HBV infections, especially in children, are asymptomatic, limiting the utility of surveillance data for estimating disease burden. 6. Population-based biomarker surveys are essential to estimate the prevalence of HBV infection, document progress, and plan effective prevention strategies. A key requirement for verification is the analysis of seroprevalence data for HBV infection markers. 7. Countries may conduct biomarker surveys of HBsAg using representative sampling of population cohorts born after the nationwide implementation of universal hepatitis B immunization programs and after sustaining high coverage with HepB3 (and HepB-BD if available). Ideally, these surveys should be conducted within three years of applying for verification. 8. According to WHO guidelines, the most appropriate study design for documenting the impact of hepatitis B immunization is a cross-sectional survey of a nationally representative population. 9. To document the impact of hepatitis B vaccination, countries should survey children aged five years or older who had the opportunity to be vaccinated and have passed through the period of highest risk for chronic infection. School-based sampling is recommended if school attendance in the target age group is at least 95%; otherwise, community-based sampling should be used. 10. WHO recommends complex survey sampling methods, such as stratified multistage cluster sampling with random selection at each stage. Detailed methodologies are available in the WHO reference manuals. 11. Key thresholds for verification include a point estimate of HBsAg seroprevalence below the target and an upper bound of the 95% confidence interval that does not exceed the target. Additional criteria for a valid biomarker survey are outlined in the relevant annexes. 12. Since biomarker surveys measure the prevalence of HBV infection among birth cohorts included in the survey, it can be assumed that with sustained hepatitis B immunization coverage, younger cohorts will not have higher HBsAg prevalence than the surveyed older cohorts. 13. Countries should provide data showing HepB3 and HepB-BD coverage for at least the most recent three years. This can be done alongside the biomarker survey if children under five years are sampled. Immunization coverage data will be analyzed at national, provincial, and district levels, as well as for specific subpopulations that may not be reached by routine immunization. 14. If evidence suggests that certain communities, such as specific ethnic groups, have a high prevalence of HBV infection, it is highly desirable to have immunization coverage data for these communities. Administrative immunization coverage data should be corroborated by survey data, such as immunization coverage surveys, Demographic Health Surveys, or Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys. 15. Countries may supplement information on data quality with findings from data quality assessments, audits, or immunization program reviews. 16. WHO recommends that all countries include a hepatitis B timely birth dose (HepB-TBD) in their national immunization schedules. For countries that have not introduced a universal birth dose, evidence of high coverage of antenatal HBV testing and TBD vaccination among infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers should be provided. 17. Countries should also provide information on national policies or guidelines on antenatal HBV testing and prevention of perinatal HBV transmission, including the availability and coverage of HBIG. Studies on PVST of infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers may also supplement this information. 18. The WHO Regional Director is responsible for appointing an independent Verification Expert Panel (VEP) composed of experts in hepatitis B control, epidemiology, immunization, surveys, laboratory science, statistics, and other relevant fields. The terms of reference, conflicts of interest, and confidentiality policies are outlined in the relevant annexes. 19. Upon receiving a request for verification, the WHO regional secretariat will establish a Regional Verification Team (RVT) consisting of a chair and two other VEP members. The chair will coordinate communication among team members and summarize the team’s recommendations. 20. Once confident that the target has been achieved based on an internal evaluation, a country may request the initiation of the verification process. This involves assembling and reviewing biomarker survey and immunization coverage data, as well as other relevant information, before submitting a formal request for verification to the WHO regional office. 21. The RVT will perform a detailed desk review of the submitted data, which can be conducted remotely. Discussions are carried out via email or teleconference, and a country visit may be undertaken if necessary. The RVT may contact the country’s focal person for verification if additional information or clarification is needed. 22. The RVT will examine evidence on a case-by-case basis, following the criteria and indicators outlined in the verification guidelines. Adjustments may be made to account for country-specific contexts, such as subnational variations in hepatitis B epidemiology or demographic characteristics. 23. The RVT may also consider additional information, including findings from its own literature review. A tool for evaluating country verification data and reference points for evaluation criteria are included in the relevant annexes. 24. The WHO Regional Director will send an official letter to the country informing them of the verification decision. The WHO Regional Office will report to technical advisory groups and the WHO Regional Committee on verified countries and may highlight these achievements in news releases or other communications. 25. To maintain verification status, countries must annually review HepB coverage data submitted in WHO/UNICEF joint reporting forms. The Regional Office will monitor progress and provide recommendations or advice on policies to sustain or achieve targets.
